transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-22 15:00 PDT
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Patel (Redwood SE), Liam O'Rourke (AcornLoop CTO), Nadia Singh (Lead ML Eng), Marcus Holt (Head of Security)

[00:00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. quick intros from our side: I'm Maya, I'm the AE covering mid-market, and Jordan's our solutions engineer.
[00:00:12] Jordan (Redwood SE): Hi, yeah hi all. I handle infra and benchmarks, so I'll likely be the one helping with the pilot.
[00:00:18] Liam (AcornLoop): Liam here, CTO at AcornLoop. We're looking to add a summarization + retrieval assistant into our product, want to understand time to first token and hosting tradeoffs.
[00:00:26] Nadia (AcornLoop): Nadia, lead ML eng — I'll own the integration and evaluation. quick note: we have a small cluster on GCP and usually prototype with hosted APIs first.
[00:00:34] Marcus (AcornLoop Security): Marcus from security — mainly here to validate compliance reqs, SSO, KMS, audit logs.

[00:00:45] Maya: Great. The purpose today is to walk through Redwood's quickstart / self-serve flow, the free credit offer and how fast you can get a prototype called TTFT — time to first token — and then talk hosting: hosted API, Redwood Dedicated reserved capacity, or Private (VPC/on-prem).
[00:01:05] Liam: Sounds good. high-level constraint: we'd like to have an internal demo within two weeks and set production criteria in about 6-8 weeks. Budget is TBD but we care about predictable latency and cost.

[00:01:25] Jordan: For the TTFT, our sandbox org usually takes under an hour to create. With the credits we provide, teams often make their first call within a day — most within a morning. Does that match your expectations?
[00:01:37] Nadia: A morning would be ideal. But we need sample prompts and a quick recipe for caching/batching recommendations if we test at scale.
[00:01:46] Maya: We'll include a quickstart guide with sample prompts + a suggested batch size and recommended model variants. We'll also suggest Redwood Optimize hints — quantization and batching settings — for cost vs latency tradeoffs.

[00:02:05] Marcus: Quick question: for the sandbox credits, is any customer data stored by Redwood? We need to know retention, encryption, and KMS options.
[00:02:15] Maya: Good call. Short answer: hosted API by default stores minimal logs for debugging for a short retention period — but you can opt out on the sandbox and we can enable no-persist mode for request bodies. For production, Dedicated and Private give stronger isolation; Private can be deployed in your VPC and use your KMS.
[00:02:37] Marcus: When you say KMS, you support customer-managed keys / HSM?
[00:02:41] Jordan: Yes — for Private we can integrate with AWS KMS or customer HSMs. For Dedicated we also support KMS integrations and larger audit log retention. Hosted supports envelope encryption with our KMS, but we can discuss custom arrangements for enterprise.

[00:03:02] Liam: About performance: the demo we're building is single-turn summarization with a 1k token context. What latencies should we expect for hosted vs dedicated?
[00:03:12] Jordan: Depends on model. For one of our mid-sized gen models, hosted 95th percentile is usually 250–400ms per 1k tokens with streaming on the path. Dedicated — if you reserve GPU pools with the right config — you can get lower P95s ~150–250ms. Private will depend on your infra, but you get control over kernel selection and quantization, so you could get similar to dedicated. We can run a bench against your prompts to give precise numbers.
[00:03:42] Nadia: Great, so we should run the benchmark with our sample prompts; we care about P95 and cost per 1k tokens.

[00:03:55] Maya: For the pilot we'll propose: 2-week benchmark, three workloads (summarization, rerank, embeddings), and we'll capture latency, throughput, and cost. Jordan will prepare the test harness you can run from your network or we can run from Redwood's infra.
[00:04:12] Liam: We prefer to run tests from our side for latency consistency. Also would like to see fallback behavior — if a dedicated pool is saturated, how do fallbacks to hosted behave?
[00:04:22] Jordan: Smart routing will fall back to compatible model variants in another region or hosted pool depending on policy. We can simulate load to show graceful degradation.

[00:04:36] Marcus: Security items: SSO (SAML / OIDC), RBAC for tokens, audit logs with export, SOC2 Type II evidence, and encryption keys. Also data residency — we need EU region hosting for some customers.
[00:04:49] Maya: We have SAML and OIDC, and RBAC support for tokens/roles in the Console. SOC2 Type II pack is in our security docs; Jordan will attach the SOC2 report and the compliance checklist. We support regional hosting for EU; Private allows strict residency guarantees.

[00:05:12] Liam: Any gotchas for integrating with our GCP-based backend?
[00:05:17] Jordan: None major. For self-serve you'll hit our REST API with an API key; we have client SDKs. If you go Private in VPC, we'll provide a private peering and a private control plane, so network egress stays inside your cloud. For Dedicated, we can colocate in the same cloud region.

[00:05:34] Nadia: About cost — can you give top-level pricing for self-serve hosted vs reserved? We need to know when it makes sense to move to Dedicated.
[00:05:44] Maya: Hosted is usage-based; you'll pay per token/embedding unit. We'll share an example cost workbook in the follow-up that maps requests per second to expected monthly spend. Dedicated is reserved commit with lower per-token pricing but a monthly/annual commitment. The breakpoint is workload dependent; Jordan will include a simple modeler in the benchmark plan.

[00:06:07] Marcus: Do you provide separate SLAs for Dedicated?
[00:06:10] Maya: Yes — Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets; Hosted has best-effort availability with strong SLOs but enterprise SLAs attach to Dedicated and Private.

[00:06:22] Liam: One thing — we prototype fast, but we also need to ensure the outputs don't hallucinate critical facts. Do you have suggested evaluations or monitoring?
[00:06:32] Jordan: We have Redwood Optimize that suggests model variants and quantization to keep quality. Also quality monitoring and regression alerts tied to prompt sets. For hallucination we recommend a reranker or retrieval-augmented approach and we'll help instrument ROUGE/QA-based checks.

[00:06:50] Nadia: Nice. For the quickstart, what do you need us to do to get TTFT within a day?
[00:06:56] Maya: Three things: (1) Accept the trial invite and create a sandbox org, (2) provide a contact to receive credits, (3) paste a couple of sample prompts so we can pre-populate the quickstart. We'll also give a small Jupyter notebook to call the API.

[00:07:12] Liam: We'll do that. Marcus — any blockers from security to doing a sandbox?
[00:07:16] Marcus: Sandbox is fine as long as it's isolated and we can opt out of storing payloads. For any PII tests we'll want no-persist and short retention.

[00:07:28] Maya: That's standard; we'll flag the org as no-persist and ensure logs are scrubbed. Jordan: I'll also include the option to run a local harness if you prefer.

[00:07:40] Liam: Competitors question — we evaluated Anthropic earlier; why pick Redwood for this phase?
[00:07:46] Maya: Two things: predictable path to production (same API and tooling across hosted/dedicated/private) and production-first controls — batching, caching, routing policies that directly impact unit economics. Also deeper observability in the Console for per-route latency/cost.
[00:08:02] Nadia: Will you support us moving from hosted to Dedicated without app changes?
[00:08:07] Jordan: Yes — deployment abstraction means you can pin model version and change routing without application changes; same REST surface and SDK.

[00:08:18] Marcus: Can you show logs and traces per token? Our auditors like token-level tracing for sensitive flows.
[00:08:24] Maya: Token-level traces are available in Redwood Console as part of our observability add-on. For Private/Dedicated you can keep full traces in your logging infra via exporters.

[00:08:36] Liam: Operationally, if we run into a regression after upgrading a model, can we roll back?
[00:08:40] Jordan: Yes — rollouts support canary deploys, A/B, and automatic fallback policies. We also tie quality monitoring to prompt sets so regressions produce alerts.

[00:08:52] Nadia: Okay let's talk specifics for the pilot. We'd like latency and cost for the summarization workload with our 1k context, plus one rerank flow and embeddings for semantic search.
[00:09:03] Jordan: We'll include those three. For the benchmark we recommend two configurations: hosted baseline and dedicated-like config (reserved pool) so you can see cost and P95 diff. We'll also provide the sample code to hit the endpoints and collect metrics.

[00:09:20] Liam: Timeline check: can you get the credits in 48 hours? We'd like to start tests Monday.
[00:09:26] Maya: Yes — I can provision the credits and email instructions today; expect an email by end of day. 
[00:09:34] Marcus: Please attach SOC2 and encryption docs when you send that.
[00:09:38] Maya: Will do.

[00:09:42] (brief cross-talk about calendar slots)

[00:09:55] Jordan: One last note — if you want to test private deployment later, we'll need to scope network connectivity, provide an installer or helm chart for on-prem, and agree on KMS. That usually has a longer lead time.
[00:10:09] Liam: Noted. For now it's self-serve hosted + credits and benchmark.
[00:10:14] Maya: Perfect. Recap: Maya sends credits and pricing workbook + SOC2 docs; Jordan sends benchmark plan and sample prompts; Nadia provides prompt templates; Marcus sends security checklist. We'll target a pilot kick-off week of 2026-08-31.
[00:10:32] Nadia: Sounds good.
[00:10:34] Liam: Thanks — looking forward to the email.
[00:10:36] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up.

[00:10:45] End of recording - remaining 35 minutes were side-channel scheduling and doc sharing not captured in transcript due to recorder quirks. Some small filler and repeat checks.
